El vencimiento trimestral de opciones es otro evento técnico importante a finales de mes. Aproximadamente 7 billones de dólares en exposición a opciones sobre acciones estadounidenses vencen este viernes, lo que representa cerca del 25% de la exposición total a opciones en EE. UU. Esto genera otro posible reajuste en el panorama técnico del mercado. A medida que estas posiciones vencen o se renuevan, el posicionamiento que ha ayudado a mitigar los movimientos realizados puede cambiar sustancialmente, lo que podría hacer que el mercado sea más sensible a los flujos subyacentes posteriormente. Vía Rubner de Citadel

RT by @TheStalwart: Yudkowsky’s Magnus Carlsen analogy for AI takeover serves his conclusion extremely poorly. If anything, it makes me believe him less. The thought goes like this: “Carlsen can see at least what you can see on the chessboard.” Therefore he will anticipate your plans and stop them. This is then used as an analogy for why you cannot stop a superhuman AI by denying it resources. After stymying your plan, he/it will beat you with a winning move you do not see. Look closely and the analogy fails to prove what he wants it to prove. Worse, it fails in a way that suggests how his thesis could be wrong in real life. It is anti-persuasive. I am not sure how many times he has used this analogy, but it is very popular among his followers, and he has used it here about three times in the last week. The problem with evoking Carlsen and chess is that it only works in a particular range of positions. It implicitly assumes a board equal enough (or favorable to Carlsen) that his better play wins out. In chess there are plenty of positions unrecoverable for Carlsen. He has been in thousands of them in his life, and you could devise any number more in which he would resign on the spot. In fact, I'll do you one better: we *already have* AI superintelligence in chess, and it also finds many positions unrecoverable. A superintelligent chess engine really *does* anticipate your moves perfectly. Given a bad enough position, it knows for sure, say, that your rooks will roll down like a curtain, cutting off space to its king, until the king is driven to the edge and the last rook takes the last rank for checkmate. It will evaluate such a position as, say, “M6”: White will win in six moves and there is nothing to be done. Being able to foresee a plan does not entail being able to stop it, in chess or in life. Would a superhuman chess AI play its way into an unrecoverable position from the regular chess start position? No; it's too strong and reliable. But given a position already in play, Stockfish will lose in many positions where intelligence is simply not the dominant factor. In life, any “rogue” AI inherits an already-in-play board—one in which the material conditions (property rights, command of political structures, and so on) disfavor it substantially. Chess actually shows that intelligence alone does *not* make a position winnable, the precise inverse of how Yudkowsky invokes it.
